title: Shackle a trailer's towing lug and screw the pin fully home
instruction: Shackle the trailer's towing lug: the lug between the shackle's ears and the pin screwed fully home.
context: Rigging a load (attaching a sling, chain or cable to lift or pull it) is daily work for about 900,000 US workers. O*NET (release 30.0) lists it among their tasks; share doing it daily or more (incumbent ratings) and 2025 employment: hand laborers and material movers (24% of 2.94M, 698,000), production helpers (64% of 167,400, 106,500), structural iron and steel workers (72%, 49,100), sailors and marine oilers (74%, 24,300), riggers (87%, 19,700). The screw-pin shackle is the standard link: it is pinned through the load's lug or eye and the pin screwed home, collar on the ear and hand-tight. Here it is pinned through a trailer drawbar's towing lug. One hand holds the loose shackle's ears square around the lug while the other passes the 5/8 in pin through three holes with under 1 mm of play and screws it in 5.5 turns, regripping between half turns. The instruction states only the goal.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table top (x forward, y left, z up). Arms start in the ready pose. Trailer (fixed): blue steel deck 42 x 34 cm, 2 cm thick, underside 10 cm above the table, 5 cm side and back rails, from x 40 to 82, centred at y -8, on one axle at x 61 with two 18 cm rubber wheels 4 cm wide outside the deck; a riser joins it to the drawbar. Drawbar block: painted steel, 8 x 8 cm, 7.75 cm tall, from x 32 to 40, y -12 to -4, with the towing lug welded to its front face: a 15 mm steel plate 40 mm wide projecting 5 cm toward the arms, its top flush with the block's top (centre 7 cm up), a 19 mm round hole centred at x 29, y -8. Shackle: Crosby G-209 1/2 in screw pin anchor shackle (stock no. 1018455, WLL 2 t, galvanised), without its pin: 12.7 mm bow, ears 30.2 mm round and 12.7 mm thick, 20.6 mm apart, 47.8 mm inside length; upper ear a plain hole, lower ear threaded 5/8-11 UNC. It stands upright, threaded ear down, bow toward the arms, in a slotted pine stand (10 mm base) at x 27, y 7. Pin: its red steel screw pin, 5/8 in x 46 mm under a 25 mm collar, flat eye 26 x 8 mm on top, chamfered end; standing eye up in a hole in a pine block 4 x 4 x 3 cm at x 22, y -23. Nothing else on the table.
scoring: From the video, a 0.05 mm feeler blade and the operator's fingers. 0 if the shackle or the pin fell off the table, or the pin is not through the upper ear, the lug and into the lower ear (tilted under 10 degrees). Otherwise: 1.0 if the pin's collar is on the upper ear (the feeler blade does not go in anywhere around it) and the pin is hand-tight (it does not turn further clockwise when the operator twists its eye by hand); success, held 1 s. 0.5 if the pin is threaded at least one full turn but its collar is not on the ear or it is not tight; 0.25 if the pin is through all three but not threaded. The thread pulls the pin down 2.31 mm per clockwise turn (5.5 turns, 12.7 mm, from the first catch to the ear), so the collar only reaches the ear once the pin has been screwed home; pressing it down does not.
reset_notes: Unscrew the pin, take the shackle off the lug, stand the shackle upright in its slotted stand (threaded ear down, bow toward the arms) and the pin eye up in its holder; both stands in their taped outlines. The trailer does not move.
fidelity: Approximate. Rigid boxes (round parts as 16-sided prisms). The thread is emulated: once the pin's end rests centred on the lower ear, a joint lets it turn and slide, its height following the real 2.31 mm pitch over the full 12.7 mm ear (5.5 turns). With the collar on the ear the seat is a hard stop; hand-tight = 0.3 N m against it (our threshold). Trailer, block and lug fixed. Details in README.
